instruction: Design a single-page SVG interface for a polished domino game called Play with Tiles. Include a central tabletop with a readable chain of matched dominoes, a player's hand or tile rack, a draw pile, turn and score indicators, and a small rule or match-value cue. Make pip counts, tile orientation, and legal continuation points instantly legible. Put strong emphasis on tactile materials, strategic clarity, balanced composition, and a distinctive, professional board-game identity.

history.critique: Brief & Intent: All required modules are present (tabletop, chain, hand, draw pile, turn/score, rule cue), but two brief-critical legibility goals fail. (1) The player's hand at the bottom is clipped by the viewport — only the top halves of the tiles show, so pip counts in the most important interactive area are not 'instantly legible.' (2) Legal continuation points are not tied to the chain: the 'MATCHING VALUE 3' pill floats at top-center while the real open ends sit at the far left/right of the row, and the 7th tile on the right is an unexplained ghosted/empty slot that reads as a broken tile rather than a play point. Clarity & Hierarchy: The primary action zone (hand) is below the fold, inverting visual priority; the chain sits in a sea of empty felt so the focal point is weak; 'TURN You' is duplicated (header pill + table pill); the rival rack wraps 6+1 like a layout bug; the scoreboard's tiny yellow/red bars are unlabeled so their meaning (progress to 100?) is unclear. Visual System & Craft: The palette (walnut/cream/felt/gold) is coherent and on-brand, but tactility is under-delivered — tiles are flat with minimal shadow, the felt is a flat muted green with no texture or vignette, the wood frame has no grain, and the chain tiles are small relative to the table, leaving large dead zones top and bottom that hurt the 'balanced composition' goal. Expressiveness & Distinctiveness: The parlor identity (serif wordmark, small-caps labels, 'DOMINO PARLOUR · DOUBLE-SIX') is a good start, but the mostly-empty green table and the stray ghost tile make the centerpiece feel generic and unfinished rather than authored; there is no memorable moment (no inlay, emblem, corner detail, or lift on the tiles). Real trade-offs: enlarging the chain and adding end markers consumes the empty felt (good — fixes craft and clarity at once); making the table shorter to fit the hand reduces felt area (acceptable, since a legible hand/chain outranks a big empty table); keeping one turn indicator loses at-a-glance header status (mitigate with a subtle status dot); turning the ghost tile into a labeled open-end slot trades a 'clean' row for explicit play-point legibility (worth it).

P1 — Un-clip the hand: restructure the vertical rhythm so the full 'Your Hand' rack is visible in a 100vh layout (shrink table height, tighten top/bottom padding, move the bottom table cue up or merge it into the hand bar).
